name: Wave Machine
miniText: NetLogo Wave Machine investigates how a driven membrane supports traveling and reflected waves. A rectangular array of vertically moving nodes interacts with four neighbors through spring-like forces; fixed edges reflect disturbances and a driver imposes sinusoidal displacement. Provides classical vibration and wave theory; the DOI identifies the Cambridge reissue [1]. Provides numerical discretization and stability context for lattice approximations to wave equations [2]. Provides a plate-mode comparison while highlighting that a spring membrane and a bending plate are different physical systems [3]. The source idealizes displacement to one direction and prescribes driver amplitude; time step, damping and lattice spacing constrain interpretation. The simulation illustrates superposition, reflection and the relation between local coupling and macroscopic wave patterns. Reproducing these patterns establishes rule fidelity, not empirical validation.

Registrant abstract consulted: John William Strutt, third Baron Rayleigh (1842–1919), was an English physicist best known as the co-discoverer of the element argon, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904. Rayleigh graduated from Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1865 and after conducting private research was appointed Cavendish Professor of Experimental Physics in 1879, a post which he held until 1884. These highly influential volumes, first published between 1877 and 1878, contain Rayleigh's classic account of acoustic theory. Bringing together contemporary research and his own experiments, Rayleigh clearly describes the origins and transmission of sound waves through different media. This textbook was considered the standard work on the subject for many years and provided the foundations of modern acoustic theory. Volume 1 discusses the origin and transmission of sound waves in harmonic vibrations, the vibrations of bars, stretched strings, plates and membranes, through mathematical models and experimental discussions.
